item.title: Error Correction in a Distributed Quantum Computer
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Real-time distributed error detection and feedforward correction demonstrated across two trapped-ion quantum processors separated by ∼2 m. Stabilises logical qubit in a [[2,1,1]] repetition code and actively corrects arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state.

Grade 0.489 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · E. M. Ainley, A. Agrawal, T. Araki, A. R. Martínez, D. Main, E. Malinowski, J. A. Blackmore, S. Chen, P. Drmota, M. Mallweger, D. P. Nadlinger, R. Srinivas, S. C. Benjamin, G. Araneda, D. M. Lucas

Figure

Remote stabiliser measurement scheme and network qubit parity readout. Network qubit parity plotted against analysis pulse phase demonstrates syndrome discrimination between +1 and −1 eigenspaces of data-qubit pairs.

Asks

Can stabiliser measurements and quantum error detection/correction be performed across spatially separated quantum processors using photonic interconnects?

But

Interleaved recooling reduces entanglement generation rate from ∼100 s−1 to ∼10 s−1. Calibration drifts and gate phase offsets not fully captured in error budget.

Tools

trapped-ion processors (⁸⁸Sr⁺, ⁴³Ca⁺) · photonic interconnects · mixed-species geometric phase gates · real-time classical feedforward (TTL link)

Abstract

Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.

item.title: Extremely Low-Cost Magic State Preparation toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Postselected infidelity scales as 210.2p3+O(p4) under uniform circuit-level depolarizing noise, bounded at 2.2×10−7 at p=10−3 (99.9% joint confidence, 86.9% acceptance) using 19 qubits and 82 CNOT gates.

Grade 0.486 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Jianshuo Gao, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao

Figure

Postselected logical infidelity versus physical depolarizing error rate p, showing exact analytical O(p3) scaling and the finite-p upper-bound certificate at p=10−3.

Asks

Can co-designing the stabilizer-generator basis with flag circuits reduce the qubit and circuit overhead of fault-tolerant magic-state preparation?

Before

100 CNOTs, 31 measurements, and leading correction error 25.5p2 in the two-block benchmark of Daguerre and Kim (2025).

But

Applies strictly to destructive postselected error-detection diagnostic; minimum-weight error correction has leading infidelity 183.81p2. Omits memory errors, routing, idle time, crosstalk, and coherent leakage.

Tools

quantum Reed-Muller to Steane code gauge fixing · jointly flagged syndrome extraction · destructive error detection · exact low-order fault enumeration · stratified Monte Carlo sampling

Abstract

Fault-tolerant preparation of non-Clifford resource states is a major contributor to the overhead of quantum computation, motivating protocols that achieve high output fidelity with minimal qubit and circuit costs. We introduce a low-cost magic-state preparation protocol in which the choice of stabilizer generators is co-designed with the flag gadgets, allowing the syndrome-extraction circuit itself to filter correlated faults across a non-Clifford layer. The protocol prepares a logical plus state in the 15-qubit quantum Reed-Muller code, applies a transversal T gate, and gauge-fixes the same register into the seven-qubit Steane code. By reorganizing equivalent Z-type stabilizer generators into jointly flagged measurement groups, the protocol eliminates all accepted logical-error contributions arising from one or two circuit faults under destructive error detection. Under a uniform circuit-level depolarizing noise model, the postselected infidelity is 210.2p³+O(p⁴). At p=10⁻³, exact low-order enumeration combined with stratified sampling bounds the infidelity by 2.2×10⁻⁷ at 99.9% joint confidence, while retaining an acceptance probability of 86.9%. The complete circuit requires only 19 qubits and 82 CNOT gates. These results demonstrate that stabilizer-generator design can substantially reduce the cost of postselected magic-state preparation, although corrected operation and the fidelity of an unmeasured output block require separate analysis.

item.title: Sparse-Blossom Decoding in o(1) Time
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Parallel sparse blossom decodes an O(d)-round syndrome extraction window on a distance-d rotated surface code in average parallel runtime bounded by exp⁡[O((log⁡log⁡d)2)], yielding o(1) average parallel runtime per round.

Grade 0.470 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Ryo Mikami, Hayata Yamasaki

Figure

Event counts per shot per syndrome extraction round plotted against code distance d∈{9,13,…,49}, demonstrating that parallel sparse-blossom runtime per round decreases with increasing d at low physical error rates.

Asks

Can minimum-weight perfect matching decoding via sparse blossom be parallelized with an exact correctness guarantee and a runtime per round that scales as o(1)?

Before

Decoding time per round scaled as O(d2.34) in sequential sparse blossom, requiring O(d3.34) total latency for a d-round window (Higgott and Gidney 2023).

But

Circuit-level local stochastic error model below a finite threshold pth, with finite-size numerical comparisons assuming negligible parallelization overhead.

Tools

parallel sparse blossom · hierarchical error clustering · minimum-weight embedded matching · rotated surface code simulation

Abstract

Matching-based decoding is widely used in quantum error correction, and accelerating it is key to enabling fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding provides rigorous guarantees for error suppression, while sparse blossom enables its practical implementation at modest problem sizes. However, the runtime of existing sparse-blossom implementations unavoidably increases with problem size, motivating a rigorous parallelization framework that guarantees correctness and a runtime shorter than the syndrome-extraction timescale. Here, we present such a framework and prove that the resulting parallel sparse-blossom algorithm produces the same correction as the original, non-parallel sparse blossom. For the rotated surface code with code distance d and physical error rates below a finite threshold, we prove that the average parallel runtime of decoding for O(d) rounds of syndrome extraction is upper bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of d. For a d-round decoding window, this implies that the average parallel runtime per round is o(1). We also perform numerical simulation to identify conditions under which the parallel runtime per round decreases with increasing code distance. These results suggest that increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding.

item.title: Modeling Quantum Error Detection with Transition Matrices
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Code-adapted basis-population dynamics under circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise are mapped to an exact (2n+1)-dimensional Markov kernel, reducing Steane code dynamics from 129 to 11 states via orbit lumping.

Grade 0.451 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Rohan S. Kumar, Ben Foxman, Yongshan Ding

Figure

Accepted logical population and rejection probabilities as a function of integer QED cycle count for the [[4,2,2]] and [[5,1,3]] codes at physical error rate ε=10−3, comparing exact transition-matrix curves with 106-shot Stim Monte Carlo data.

Asks

At what granularity can the multi-cycle dynamics and post-selection of quantum error detection protocols under noise be modeled exactly and tractably?

But

Restricted to circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise and data-preserving Clifford syndrome-extraction circuits; transition matrix scales as 2n+1 before symmetry lumping.

Tools

Markov transition matrices · stabilizer code-adapted basis · absorbing Markov chain reduction · Markov orbit lumping · Stim Monte Carlo simulations

Abstract

We construct an explicit transition matrix that exactly describes code-adapted basis-population dynamics of stabilizer codes under circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise. The matrix is expressed in a code-adapted basis that captures probability flow between logical-basis labels and syndrome sectors. For quantum error detection (QED), we incorporate post-selection by aggregating rejected outcomes into an absorbing state, so that a single transition matrix represents a full clock cycle of gates, syndrome extraction, and post-selection. Additionally, we characterize when protocol symmetries permit exact lumping to simpler, more interpretable models. The transition matrix framework enables direct application of classical stochastic-matrix techniques to analyze multi-cycle QED protocols. First, we identify a leading-order obstruction to a stationary logical-only accepted-map description, and quantify the accepted leakage injection from QED-check imperfections that causes it. Second, we express leading-order QED efficiency as a function of check frequency in terms of physically meaningful parameters, and prove that less frequent checks improve efficiency to leading order. We evaluate the framework on the [[4,2,2]] and [[5,1,3]] codes under depolarizing gate noise and readout errors: transition-matrix predictions agree with million-shot Stim Monte Carlo at the scale of the reported confidence intervals, and matrix-computed results illustrate the first-cycle transient and interval-dependent efficiency. More broadly, the transition-matrix formalism provides both an analytical foundation for QED analysis and an interpretable tool for understanding code behavior under realistic noise.

item.title: Testing and Diagnosing Parameter Miscalibration in Probabilistic Error Cancellation via Direct Fidelity Estimation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — DFE overlap Y≡Tr⁡(ρρ~) and purity 𝒫≡Tr⁡(ρ~2) of PEC-mitigated state ρ~ serve as hardware witnesses and directional diagnostics: consistent underestimation yields Y≤1 and 𝒫≤1, while consistent overestimation yields Y≥1 and 𝒫≥1.

Grade 0.439 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Francesc Sabater, Tristan Kraft, Carlos A. Riofrío, Barbara Kraus

Figure

DFE overlap Tr⁡(ρ~ρ) plotted against assumed depolarizing parameter p~e for N=50 qubits and s=50,100,150 gates. The curve crosses 1 exactly at the true parameter pe=0.02, being <1 for underestimated p~e and >1 for overestimated p~e.

Asks

How to test whether the noise parameters used in Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) are accurate directly on hardware, and diagnose whether they are overestimated or underestimated?

But

Requires positive Pauli fidelities (>1/2 identity coefficient) and absence of hybrid miscalibration; overestimation directionality for Y in arbitrary circuits holds perturbatively under a nondegeneracy condition, while purity condition 𝒫 holds non-perturbatively.

Tools

Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) · Two-copy purity estimator · Classically simulable surrogate circuits

Abstract

Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) is a standard technique for mitigating noise in quantum computations, but its unbiasedness relies on accurate knowledge of the underlying noise parameters. In practice, these parameters are inferred from experimental data and may be inaccurate. We introduce a protocol that tests PEC parameter consistency on hardware by applying Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) to the effective mitigated state. The resulting DFE overlap serves not only as a witness of parameter miscalibration but, under appropriate conditions, also reveals whether the PEC parameters have been overestimated or underestimated. We establish this behavior for arbitrary circuits under global depolarizing noise and for Clifford circuits under general Pauli-stochastic noise. For arbitrary circuits subject to Pauli-stochastic noise, the underestimation result holds generally, while the corresponding overestimation result is established perturbatively for sufficiently small consistent miscalibrations under an additional nondegeneracy condition. We further show that the purity of the effective mitigated operator provides a more general diagnostic, allowing the miscalibration direction to be identified for arbitrary circuits and arbitrary parameter deviations. Finally, we describe a two-copy PEC procedure for measuring this quantity and show that, together with the DFE overlap, it determines the Hilbert-Schmidt distance from the ideal state. The sampling overhead incurred by our protocol is the same as that of PEC, and we discuss strategies to improve it.

item.title: Benchmarking the computational power of quantum computers
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Defines QUOPS to benchmark quantum capability by circuit size and execution rate. Translating utility challenge problems (factoring RSA-2048, FeMoco) shows computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude over current physical processors (Quantinuum Helios-1 Q=1504, H2-1 Q=1320).

Grade 0.438 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Timothy Proctor, Oliver Hart, Oliver Widzowski Maupin, Matthew Girling, Daniel Hothem, Daniel Mills, Jordan Hines, Karl Mayer, Jacob S. Nelson, Tyler LeBlond, Zohim Chandani, Diego Forlivesi, Piper C. Wysocki, Boldizsár Poór, Joan M. Dreiling, Annie Park, Adam P. Reed, Brian Estey, Cameron Foltz, Akhil Isanaka, M. S. Allman, Michael Mills, Maxwell D. Urmey, Peter E. Siegfried, Audrey Faricy, Jin-Sung Kim, Cristina Cîrstoiu, Andrew D. Baczewski, Charles H. Baldwin, Robin Blume-Kohout

Figure

Plots QUOPS capability regions (circuit size vs width), historical capability score scaling vs time with exponential trend lines showing 1.4-year (Quantinuum) and 2.1-year (IBM) doubling times, and QUOPS execution rate vs score for physical, logical, and projected architectures against utility milestones.

Asks

How can quantum computational power be directly benchmarked and compared across disparate physical and logical architectures relative to utility-scale challenge problems?

Before

Quantum volume and physical gate error rates; quantum volume scaling requires exponential classical verification and does not map directly to fault-tolerant utility resource requirements.

But

Historical score inferences rely on global depolarizing noise, two-qubit gates as the sole error source, and simplified compilation models accurate to within roughly a factor of two.

Tools

QUOPS benchmark suite · Mirror circuit fidelity estimation · Steane llbracket7,1,3rrbracket logical processor · Quantinuum Helios-1 ion-trap processor · IBM ibm_boston and Google Willow superconducting processors

Abstract

Quantum computing hardware is advancing rapidly toward utility-scale machines that will enable scientific breakthroughs. Many teams are pursuing distinct and difficult-to-compare routes to this goal, using different qubit technologies and logical architectures. Tracking progress toward quantum utility therefore requires rigorous benchmarks that measure computational capability relative to utility-scale challenge problems and enable fair comparison across disparate platforms. Here we demonstrate direct, cross-platform measurement of quantum computational capability using a new benchmark that quantifies the size of the largest computationally relevant quantum circuits that a machine can execute successfully and the speed at which it can execute them. We apply this quantum universal operation performance system (QUOPS) experimentally to leading processors from Quantinuum, Google, and IBM, computing directly on physical qubits. Translating state-of-the-art resource requirements for recognized challenge problems that represent useful quantum computation into effective QUOPS circuit sizes shows that computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude, motivating fault-tolerant approaches. We use the same benchmark to assess the performance of a simple fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor implemented on up to eight [[7,1,3]]-encoded logical qubits using Quantinuum Helios-1, and project the growth of capability across successive generations of fault-tolerant quantum computers to show how QUOPS can track progress toward quantum scientific utility.

item.title: Reinforcement Learning for Syndrome Extraction
item.description:
Worth a look new method — FastSched uses reinforcement learning and importance sampling to synthesize syndrome extraction schedules, reducing logical error rate by 25.9% versus AlphaSyndrome and 71.7% versus PropHunt on average, reaching a 97.8% reduction for distance-15 surface codes.

Grade 0.429 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance” · John Zhuoyang Ye, Aarav Pabla, Jens Palsberg

Figure

Logical error rate on a logarithmic vertical axis versus rotated surface-code distance from 3 to 15 on the horizontal axis. FastSched maintains lower logical error rates than AlphaSyndrome and PropHunt across all evaluated code distances.

Asks

How can automatic schedule synthesis find quantum error correction syndrome extraction schedules with low logical error rates without sacrificing scalability to large code distances?

Before

AlphaSyndrome (MCTS) and PropHunt (MaxSAT) synthesized schedules matching or improving hand-designed baselines, but suffered from poor scaling at large distance or degraded logical error rates.

But

Evaluated under simulated noise models (e.g. Brisbane noise), one noisy extraction round, ideal boundaries, and specific decoders (PyMatching, BP-OSD). Search ceilings capped at 10 to 30 minutes.

Tools

Reinforcement learning · Importance sampling · Proximal policy optimization (PPO) · Rare-event estimation

Abstract

A key subtask of quantum error correction is to extract a syndrome that, if nontrivial, signals an error. The number of possible ways to extract a syndrome grows exponentially with the syndrome size, and these implementations vary greatly in fault tolerance, as measured by their logical error rates. This creates a natural search problem: find an implementation with a low logical error rate. Previous work solves this problem but sacrifices either solution quality or scalability. In this paper, we use reinforcement learning and importance sampling to outperform previous work at all scales. Compared with the state of the art automatic scheduling tools AlphaSyndrome and PropHunt, our tool reduces the logical error rate by 25.9% and 71.7% on average, respectively, culminating with a reduction of 97.8% for a surface code with distance 15.

item.title: Composing Detector Error Models
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Every detector in a composed stabilizer circuit splits across serial boundaries via virtual syndromes; composing gadget Extended Detector Error Models (EDEMs) under QtAt−1+PtCt−1=0 reproduces the monolithic detector error model as a block lower bidiagonal matrix dt=Dtft+(QtBt−1+PtEt−1)ft−1.

Grade 0.403 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Vadym Kliuchnikov, Justin Lietz, Fernando Pastawski

Figure

Sequential sliding-window decoding across a chain of gadget calls. Matrix columns represent fault partitions 𝖥t and rows represent detector partitions 𝖣t, forming a block-banded structure where committed corrections fold across window boundaries.

Asks

How can detector error models be constructed incrementally and modularly from reusable logical gadgets without reanalyzing the full physical circuit?

Before

Stim and stimflow compose chunk relations to reconstruct the monolithic circuit, then derive the DEM globally.

But

Stabilizer circuits with stochastic Pauli noise. Connected ports must share matching stabilizer codes and code presentations.

Tools

Extended Detector Error Models (EDEMs) · linear maps over F₂ · virtual syndromes · block-matrix diagrammatic contraction

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum programs thread together reusable logical operations, yet correcting errors requires comparing measurements across operation boundaries. Correlations tie each operation's error analysis to the computation around it. Adaptive computation makes this a runtime challenge: measurement results determine which operation comes next, so the error analysis must keep pace with execution. We introduce extended detector error models (EDEMs), which compose in sequence and in parallel, mirroring the composition of physical realizations and their detector contracts. We prove how detectors, the measurement parities used to diagnose errors, can be split across circuit boundaries, and establish conditions under which composition recovers the assembled circuit's detector error model. This structure supports symbolic precompilation and analysis of entire families of circuits. It also defines error models for decoding windows and the boundary information through which committed corrections affect subsequent windows. The same interface thus connects the design of individual logical operations to the decoding of an unfolding quantum program.
